summary: This brief report by Grillon and colleagues tests whether acute social stress increases anxiety in humans, using fear-potentiated startle measured in the dark. Twenty healthy volunteers were tested in a stress session (speech plus backward counting) and a control session. Startle was facilitated by darkness, and this facilitation was larger after the social stressor, alongside increases in cortisol, α-amylase, blood pressure, heart rate and subjective distress. The authors conclude that stress potentiates anxiety and suggest a glucocorticoid and CRH mechanism in limbic structures.
one_line: Study showing that an acute social stressor potentiates startle-measured anxiety in healthy humans tested in darkness.
key_facts: The study was published as a Brief Report titled 'Acute Stress Potentiates Anxiety in Humans' with authors Christian Grillon, Roman Duncko, Matthew F. Covington, Lori Kopperman and Mitchel A. Kling.
Participants were 20 medically and psychiatrically healthy volunteers, 9 of them men, with an average age of 28.1 years (SD = 8.3 years).
The social stressor was a 10-min task consisting of delivering a speech followed by a backward counting task.
The study used a between-subject design counterbalanced across subjects, with one session after the social stressor (stress) and one after no stressor (control), a week apart.
The FSD test started 25 min after the stressor ended.
Startle was significantly facilitated in the dark, and this facilitation was potentiated by prior exposure to the social stressor.
The Illumination main effect was F(1,18) = 15.9, p < .0009, and the Stress Condition × Illumination interaction was F(1,18) = 6.4, p < .02.
Significant fear-potentiated startle (FSD) was found in the control condition [F(1,19) = 6.8, p < .02] and in the stress condition [F(1,19) = 18.5, p < .0009].
The social stressor induced increases in salivary cortisol and α-amylase, as well as increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and subjective distress.
The authors state this is the first report showing that unconditioned anxiety is enhanced by prior stress in humans.
The authors suggest the effect may be mediated by glucocorticoid effects on corticotropin-releasing hormone in limbic structures.
The light-enhanced startle effect in the rat is mediated by CRH in the BNST, suggesting the darkness effect on startle in humans is also mediated by CRH acting on BNST receptors.
The Background notes that stress is an important factor in the development and maintenance of anxiety disorders.
